source.text: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ בְנֵֽי־הַנְּבִיאִ֖ים אֶל־אֱלִישָׁ֑ע הִנֵּֽה־נָ֣א הַמָּק֗וֹם אֲשֶׁ֨ר אֲנַ֜חְנוּ יֹשְׁבִ֥ים שָׁ֛ם לְפָנֶ֖יךָ צַ֥ר מִמֶּֽנּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] sons of the prophets to Elisha, Look, please, the place where we [are] dwelling there before you [is] too cramped for us.

en.L: And the sons of the prophets said to Elisha, "Look, please, the place where we are living before you is too cramped for us.
en.B: The company of prophets said to Elisha, "Look, the place where we live under your leadership is too small for us.
en.R: The group of prophets said to Elisha, "We live here and meet with you, but this place is too small for us.

decisions.choice: the sons of the prophets: a community of prophets
decisions.reason: "Sons of" here means members of a group, not children. These prophets lived and learned together around Elisha, as earlier around Elijah (2:3, 5, 15; 4:1, 38).

decisions.choice: dwelling before you: living under Elisha's leadership
alternatives: the place where we sit in front of you (only the meeting place)
decisions.reason: To "sit before" someone describes disciples gathered around a teacher (4:38; Ezekiel 8:1). The place is the prophets' shared dwelling and meeting place, where Elisha leads them.

decisions.choice: company of prophets; group of prophets
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for this group: "sons of the prophets" at Literal, "company of prophets" at Balanced, "group of prophets" at Readable.

decisions.choice: the speech continues into verse 2
decisions.reason: The prophets' words run on into the next verse, so the quotation stays open at the end of this record.

source.text: נֵֽלְכָה־נָּ֣א עַד־הַיַּרְדֵּ֗ן וְנִקְחָ֤ה מִשָּׁם֙ אִ֚ישׁ קוֹרָ֣ה אֶחָ֔ת וְנַעֲשֶׂה־לָּ֥נוּ שָׁ֛ם מָק֖וֹם לָשֶׁ֣בֶת שָׁ֑ם וַיֹּ֖אמֶר לֵֽכוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Let us go, please, to the Jordan, and let us take from there each [man] one beam, and let us make for ourselves there a place to dwell there. And he said, Go.

en.L: Let us go, please, to the Jordan, and let us take from there each [man] one beam, and let us make for ourselves there a place to live there." And he said, "Go."
en.B: Please let us go down to the Jordan. Each of us can take a log from there, and we can build ourselves a place to live there." He said, "Go."
en.R: Let us go to the Jordan River. Each of us can cut a log there, and we can build a place to live." Elisha said, "Go ahead."

decisions.choice: beam: a log for building
decisions.reason: The word names a roof beam or a log used in building (2 Chronicles 3:7). Each man would cut one log, so the work would be shared among them.

decisions.choice: the Jordan: the river valley near Jericho
decisions.reason: The prophets' community was near Jericho and Gilgal (2:4-5; 4:38). The Jordan valley had thickets of trees along its banks (Jeremiah 12:5), close enough to cut and carry logs.

decisions.choice: Elisha said
decisions.reason: Readable names Elisha as the speaker, since the Hebrew only has "he said".

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הָֽאֶחָ֔ד ה֥וֹאֶל נָ֖א וְלֵ֣ךְ אֶת־עֲבָדֶ֑יךָ וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אֲנִ֥י אֵלֵֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said the one, Be willing, please, and go with your servants. And he said, I will go.

en.L: And the one said, "Be willing, please, and go with your servants." And he said, "I will go."
en.B: Then one of them said, "Please be willing to come with your servants." "I will come," he answered.
en.R: Then one of them said, "Please come with us, your servants." Elisha answered, "I will come."

decisions.choice: your servants: a polite way of saying "us"
decisions.reason: The prophets call themselves Elisha's servants out of respect for him as their master (verse 5), as people do when speaking to someone they honor (Genesis 18:3; 1 Samuel 20:7-8).

decisions.choice: be willing: a polite, urgent request
decisions.reason: The verb means to agree or to be pleased to do something (Judges 19:6). The prophet asks Elisha kindly to come, and Elisha's presence turns out to matter (verses 5-7).

decisions.choice: your servants
decisions.reason: "Your servants" is kept at every level, as for polite self-reference elsewhere (1 Samuel 20). Readable adds "us" so the reader sees that the speaker means himself and the group.

source.text: וַיֵּ֖לֶךְ אִתָּ֑ם וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ הַיַּרְדֵּ֔נָה וַֽיִּגְזְר֖וּ הָעֵצִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And he went with them; and they came to the Jordan, and they cut down the trees.

en.L: And he went with them; and they came to the Jordan, and they cut down the trees.
en.B: So he went along with them. Once they reached the Jordan, they began cutting down trees.
en.R: So he went with them. When they reached the Jordan River, they started cutting down trees.

decisions.choice: they cut down: the work began
decisions.reason: The verb reports the work the group came to do. The next verse tells what happened while it was going on, so the sense is that they set about cutting trees.

decisions.choice: began cutting down; started cutting down
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that the cutting was still under way when the axe head fell (verse 5).

source.text: וַיְהִ֤י הָֽאֶחָד֙ מַפִּ֣יל הַקּוֹרָ֔ה וְאֶת־הַבַּרְזֶ֖ל נָפַ֣ל אֶל־הַמָּ֑יִם וַיִּצְעַ֥ק וַיֹּ֛אמֶר אֲהָ֥הּ אֲדֹנִ֖י וְה֥וּא שָׁאֽוּל׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, the one [was] felling the beam, and the iron fell into the water; and he cried out and said, Alas, my lord, and it [was] borrowed.

en.L: And it happened, [as] the one was felling the beam, the iron fell into the water; and he cried out and said, "Alas, my lord! And it was borrowed!"
en.B: As one of them was felling a log, the axe head fell into the water. He cried out, "Oh no, my master! It was borrowed!"
en.R: As one man was cutting down a tree, the iron head of his axe came off and fell into the water. He cried out, "Oh no, master! It was borrowed!"

decisions.choice: the iron: the iron head of an axe
decisions.reason: The Hebrew simply says "the iron". The context shows it was the head of the axe that the man was using to fell the tree (Deuteronomy 19:5 describes the same accident).

decisions.choice: borrowed: the loss was a debt the man could not easily pay
decisions.reason: The word means "asked for", that is, borrowed. Iron tools were costly, and the prophets were poor (4:1, 38-42). Losing a borrowed axe head meant a debt to its owner (Exodus 22:13), which could bring hardship like that of the widow in 4:1.

decisions.choice: the iron fell: the iron is the subject
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts a marker before "the iron" that usually points to an object, but here the iron is clearly what fell. The marker draws attention to it.

decisions.choice: Oh no
decisions.reason: The cry of dismay is put in natural modern words rather than the older "Alas". Literal keeps "Alas".

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אִישׁ־הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים אָ֣נָה נָפָ֑ל וַיַּרְאֵ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־הַמָּק֔וֹם וַיִּקְצָב־עֵץ֙ וַיַּשְׁלֶךְ־שָׁ֔מָּה וַיָּ֖צֶף הַבַּרְזֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] man of God, Where did it fall? And he showed him the place; and he cut off a stick and threw [it] there, and he made float the iron.

en.L: And the man of God said, "Where did it fall?" And he showed him the place; and he cut off a stick and threw [it] there, and he made the iron float.
en.B: The man of God asked, "Where did it fall?" When the man showed him the place, Elisha cut off a stick, threw it in there, and made the iron float.
en.R: The man of God asked, "Where did it fall?" The man showed him the place. Then Elisha cut a stick and threw it into the water there, and he made the iron head float to the top.

decisions.choice: he made the iron float: a miracle done through Elisha
decisions.reason: Iron sinks, so the iron rising to the surface is a sign of God's power at work through his prophet. The small kindness to a poor prophet fits the other signs in these chapters (2:19-22; 4:1-7, 38-44).

decisions.choice: a stick thrown into the water
decisions.reason: Elisha uses a simple object, as with the salt in the spring (2:21) and the flour in the pot (4:41). Moses too threw a piece of wood into bitter water and it became sweet (Exodus 15:25). The stick has no power of its own; the sign comes from God.

decisions.choice: the man; Elisha
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses only "he" for both men. Balanced and Readable name who does what.

source.text: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר הָ֣רֶם לָ֑ךְ וַיִּשְׁלַ֥ח יָד֖וֹ וַיִּקָּחֵֽהוּ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And he said, Lift [it] up for yourself. And he stretched out his hand and took it.

en.L: And he said, "Lift [it] up for yourself." And he stretched out his hand and took it.
en.B: "Pick it up," he said. So the man reached out his hand and took it.
en.R: Elisha said, "Pick it up." So the man reached out and took it.

decisions.choice: for yourself: the man takes back what was lost
decisions.reason: The words "for yourself" stress that the man himself recovers the axe head; Elisha does not hand it back but lets him take it from the water.

decisions.choice: the man; Elisha
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speakers, since the Hebrew has only "he".

source.text: וּמֶ֣לֶךְ אֲרָ֔ם הָיָ֥ה נִלְחָ֖ם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיִּוָּעַץ֙ אֶל־עֲבָדָ֣יו לֵאמֹ֗ר אֶל־מְק֛וֹם פְּלֹנִ֥י אַלְמֹנִ֖י תַּחֲנֹתִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] king of Aram was fighting against Israel; and he took counsel with his servants, saying, At [the] place of such [and] such [will be] my encampment.

en.L: And [the] king of Aram was fighting against Israel; and he took counsel with his servants, saying, "At such and such a place [will be] my camp."
en.B: Now the king of Aram was at war with Israel. After consulting with his officials, he said, "I will set up my camp at such and such a place."
en.R: At that time the king of Aram was at war with Israel. He made plans with his officials and told them, "I will set up my camp in a certain place."

decisions.choice: my camp: where the king meant to station his troops
alternatives: you will go down (to that place)
decisions.reason: This word for "camp" is found only here. It seems to come from the verb for camping, so the king names the place where his forces will lie in wait. A small change in the letters would give "you will go down" or "you will hide", which would match the warning in verse 9.

decisions.choice: such and such a place: the place is left unnamed
decisions.reason: The phrase is a way of saying "a certain place" without naming it (Ruth 4:1; 1 Samuel 21:3). The writer does not say where the camp was; what matters is that every place was told to Elisha.

decisions.choice: the king of Aram: the ruler of Damascus
decisions.reason: Aram was the kingdom to the northeast, centered on Damascus, often at war with Israel in these years (1 Kings 20; 22). This king is not named here; in verse 24 the king who besieges Samaria is Ben-hadad.

decisions.choice: officials
decisions.reason: The king's "servants" were his court officials and commanders: "servants" at Literal, "officials" at Balanced and Readable, as for court officials elsewhere.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֞ח אִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים אֶל־מֶ֤לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הִשָּׁ֕מֶר מֵעֲבֹ֖ר הַמָּק֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה כִּֽי־שָׁ֖ם אֲרָ֥ם נְחִתִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent [the] man of God to [the] king of Israel, saying, Take care from passing the place the this, for there Aram [are] going down.

en.L: And the man of God sent to [the] king of Israel, saying, "Take care not to pass this place, for there Aram [is] going down."
en.B: But the man of God sent this message to the king of Israel: "Take care not to pass by this place, because the Arameans are going down there."
en.R: But the man of God sent a message to the king of Israel. He said, "Be careful not to go past that place. The Arameans are going down there."

decisions.choice: going down: moving down to that place
decisions.reason: This form is found only here and seems to come from a verb meaning "go down". The Arameans were coming down to the place to set an ambush. Some read it as a form meaning "lying hidden", which gives much the same picture.

decisions.choice: the man of God knows the plan: God reveals it to him
decisions.reason: The Aramean king's plans were made in private (verse 12). Elisha knows them because God shows them to his prophet (Amos 3:7).

decisions.choice: the Arameans
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "Aram", the name of the nation used for its army. Balanced and Readable say "the Arameans".

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֞ח מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֶֽל־הַמָּק֞וֹם אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָֽמַר־ל֧וֹ אִישׁ־הָאֱלֹהִ֛ים וְהִזְהִיר֖וֹ וְנִשְׁמַ֣ר שָׁ֑ם לֹ֥א אַחַ֖ת וְלֹ֥א שְׁתָּֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent [the] king of Israel to the place which told him [the] man of God, and he warned him, and he was on guard there, not once and not twice.

en.L: And the king of Israel sent to the place that the man of God had told him [about]; and he would warn him, and he would be on guard there, not once and not twice.
en.B: So the king of Israel sent word to the place that the man of God had named to him. Time and again Elisha warned him, and the king was on his guard there, not once or twice only.
en.R: So the king of Israel sent men to the place the man of God had told him about. This happened again and again. Elisha warned the king, and the king was ready for the Arameans.

decisions.choice: he would warn ... he would be on guard: something that happened repeatedly
decisions.reason: The verb forms describe a repeated pattern, which the closing words "not once and not twice" confirm: Elisha warned the king many times, and each time the king took care.

decisions.choice: not once and not twice: many times
decisions.reason: The phrase means "more than once or twice", that is, again and again.

decisions.choice: sent: sent men or a message to the place
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not say what the king sent. He either sent troops to guard the place or a warning to the people there; either way the Arameans' plan failed.

decisions.choice: sent men; was ready for the Arameans
decisions.reason: Readable supplies "men" as what the king sent and says plainly what being on guard meant.

source.text: וַיִּסָּעֵר֙ לֵ֣ב מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֔ם עַל־הַדָּבָ֖ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַיִּקְרָ֤א אֶל־עֲבָדָיו֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֔ם הֲלוֹא֙ תַּגִּ֣ידוּ לִ֔י מִ֥י מִשֶּׁלָּ֖נוּ אֶל־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And was stormy [the] heart of [the] king of Aram over the matter the this; and he called to his servants and said to them, Will you not tell me who from [those] who [are] ours [is] for [the] king of Israel?

en.L: And the heart of [the] king of Aram was stormy over this matter; and he called his servants and said to them, "Will you not tell me who of those who [are] ours [is] for [the] king of Israel?"
en.B: This deeply troubled the king of Aram. He called his officials and said to them, "Will you not tell me which of us is on the side of the king of Israel?"
en.R: The king of Aram was very upset about this. He called his officials together and asked them, "Which one of you is helping the king of Israel? Tell me!"

decisions.choice: his heart was stormy: he was deeply disturbed
decisions.reason: The verb is used of a sea whipped by a storm (Jonah 1:11). The king's mind was in turmoil and anger because his plans kept failing.

decisions.choice: who of ours is for the king of Israel: who is a traitor
decisions.reason: The king suspects that one of his own men is secretly on Israel's side and passing on his plans.

decisions.choice: Which one of you ... Tell me!
decisions.reason: Readable puts the question first and turns the rest into a command, to keep the sentence short.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אַחַ֣ד מֵֽעֲבָדָ֔יו ל֖וֹא אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ כִּֽי־אֱלִישָׁ֤ע הַנָּבִיא֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל יַגִּיד֙ לְמֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת־הַ֨דְּבָרִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר תְּדַבֵּ֖ר בַּחֲדַ֥ר מִשְׁכָּבֶֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said one of his servants, No, my lord the king, for Elisha the prophet who [is] in Israel tells [the] king of Israel the words which you speak in [the] room of your lying down.

en.L: And one of his servants said, "No, my lord the king, for Elisha the prophet who [is] in Israel tells [the] king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom."
en.B: One of his officials answered, "None of us, my lord the king. It is Elisha, the prophet in Israel. Even the words you speak in your bedroom, he reports to the king of Israel."
en.R: One of his officials answered, "None of us, Your Majesty. It is Elisha, the prophet in Israel. He tells the king of Israel even the words you say in your bedroom."

decisions.choice: No: none of us is a traitor
decisions.reason: The single word "No" denies the king's suspicion: no one in his court is on Israel's side.

decisions.choice: the room where you lie down: your most private place
decisions.reason: The bedroom is the place where words are spoken most privately (Ecclesiastes 10:20). Even what the king says there is known to Elisha.

decisions.choice: Elisha the prophet: his fame has reached Aram
decisions.reason: The Aramean official knows Elisha by name, perhaps through the healing of Naaman, the commander of Aram's army (chapter 5).

decisions.choice: Your Majesty
decisions.reason: "My lord the king" is the formal way to address a king. Readable uses the modern form of address.

source.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר לְכ֤וּ וּרְאוּ֙ אֵיכֹ֣ה ה֔וּא וְאֶשְׁלַ֖ח וְאֶקָּחֵ֑הוּ וַיֻּגַּד־ל֥וֹ לֵאמֹ֖ר הִנֵּ֥ה בְדֹתָֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, Go and see where he [is], and I will send and take him. And it was told to him, saying, Look, in Dothan.

en.L: And he said, "Go and see where he [is], so that I may send and take him." And it was told to him, saying, "Look, [he is] in Dothan."
en.B: The king said, "Go and find out where he is, so that I can send men to seize him." Word came back to him: "He is in Dothan."
en.R: The king said, "Go and find out where Elisha is. Then I will send soldiers to capture him." Someone told the king, "He is in the town of Dothan."

decisions.choice: Dothan: a town north of Samaria
decisions.reason: Dothan lay about 10 miles north of Samaria, on the route through the hills. Joseph's brothers had once grazed their flocks there (Genesis 37:17).

decisions.choice: so that I may send and take him: the king's purpose
decisions.reason: The two verbs after "go and see" state what the king means to do once he knows where Elisha is: send men to seize him.

decisions.choice: send men; send soldiers
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whom the king would send, as verse 14 shows.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלַח־שָׁ֛מָּה סוּסִ֥ים וְרֶ֖כֶב וְחַ֣יִל כָּבֵ֑ד וַיָּבֹ֣אוּ לַ֔יְלָה וַיַּקִּ֖פוּ עַל־הָעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: And he sent there horses and chariotry and an army heavy; and they came by night and surrounded the city.

en.L: And he sent there horses and chariots and a heavy army; and they came by night and surrounded the city.
en.B: So he sent horses and chariots there, a large force. They came by night and surrounded the city.
en.R: So the king sent a big army there, with horses and chariots. They came during the night and surrounded the town.

decisions.choice: a heavy army: a large, strong force
decisions.reason: "Heavy" here means great in number and strength (1 Kings 10:2). The king sends a whole army to seize one prophet.

decisions.choice: by night: to take the town by surprise
decisions.reason: The troops arrived in the dark so that by morning the town would be shut in before anyone could escape (verse 15).

decisions.choice: a big army there, with horses and chariots
decisions.reason: Readable names the army first and adds the horses and chariots after it, to keep the sentence simple.

source.text: וַ֠יַּשְׁכֵּם מְשָׁרֵ֨ת אִ֥ישׁ הָֽאֱלֹהִים֮ לָקוּם֒ וַיֵּצֵ֕א וְהִנֵּה־חַ֛יִל סוֹבֵ֥ב אֶת־הָעִ֖יר וְס֣וּס וָרָ֑כֶב וַיֹּ֨אמֶר נַעֲר֥וֹ אֵלָ֛יו אֲהָ֥הּ אֲדֹנִ֖י אֵיכָ֥ה נַֽעֲשֶֽׂה׃

records.literal_gloss: And rose early [the] attendant of [the] man of God to arise and went out, and look, an army surrounding the city, and horse and chariotry; and said his servant to him, Alas, my lord, how will we do?

en.L: And the attendant of the man of God rose early to get up and went out, and look, an army [was] surrounding the city, with horses and chariots; and his servant said to him, "Alas, my lord! How will we act?"
en.B: When the servant of the man of God got up early in the morning and went out, there was an army with horses and chariots surrounding the city. His servant said to Elisha, "Oh no, my master! What shall we do?"
en.R: Early the next morning the servant of the man of God got up and went outside. He saw an army with horses and chariots all around the town. He said to Elisha, "Oh no, master! What are we going to do?"

decisions.choice: attendant; servant: Elisha's personal helper
decisions.reason: Two words describe the same man: one who waits on a master, and a young man in service. He is not named. Gehazi had been Elisha's servant (4:12), but he was struck with skin disease in 5:27, so this may be someone else.

decisions.choice: how will we do: what can we do
decisions.reason: The question is a cry of despair: there seems to be no way out.

decisions.choice: look: what the servant saw
decisions.reason: The word "look" (hinneh) shows the scene through the servant's eyes as he steps outside.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "servant" for both words, since they name the same man.

source.text: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אַל־תִּירָ֑א כִּ֤י רַבִּים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתָּ֔נוּ מֵאֲשֶׁ֖ר אוֹתָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, Do not fear, for many [are those] who [are] with us more than [those] who [are] with them.

en.L: And he said, "Do not fear, for those who [are] with us are more than those who [are] with them."
en.B: "Do not be afraid," Elisha answered. "There are more with us than there are with them."
en.R: Elisha answered, "Do not be afraid. There are more on our side than on theirs."

decisions.choice: those with us: God's unseen army
decisions.reason: Elisha means the heavenly forces that verse 17 shows: God's army is greater than any human army (2 Chronicles 32:7, where Hezekiah says the same of Assyria).

decisions.choice: Do not fear: God's word to those facing danger
decisions.reason: The words echo what Moses said to Israel at the sea (Exodus 14:13) and what God says to his people in many places (Genesis 15:1; Joshua 10:8).

decisions.choice: more on our side than on theirs
decisions.reason: Readable says the same comparison in shorter, plainer words.

source.text: וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֤ל אֱלִישָׁע֙ וַיֹּאמַ֔ר יְהוָ֕ה פְּקַח־נָ֥א אֶת־עֵינָ֖יו וְיִרְאֶ֑ה וַיִּפְקַ֤ח יְהוָה֙ אֶת־עֵינֵ֣י הַנַּ֔עַר וַיַּ֗רְא וְהִנֵּ֨ה הָהָ֜ר מָלֵ֨א סוּסִ֥ים וְרֶ֛כֶב אֵ֖שׁ סְבִיבֹ֥ת אֱלִישָֽׁע׃

records.literal_gloss: And prayed Elisha and said, Yahweh, open, please, his eyes, and he will see. And opened Yahweh [the] eyes of the young man, and he saw, and look, the hill [was] full [of] horses and chariotry of fire all around Elisha.

en.L: And Elisha prayed and said, "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, please open his eyes, so that he may see." And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and look, the hill [was] full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
en.B: Then Elisha prayed, "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, please open his eyes so that he can see." {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} opened the young man's eyes, and he saw that the hill was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
en.R: Then Elisha prayed, "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, please open his eyes so that he can see." So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} opened the young man's eyes. He looked and saw that the hillside all around Elisha was full of horses and chariots made of fire.

decisions.choice: open his eyes: let him see what is really there
decisions.reason: The heavenly army was already present; the servant could not see it. God lets him see the unseen world (Numbers 22:31, where Balaam's eyes are opened to see the angel).

decisions.choice: horses and chariots of fire
decisions.reason: Chariots and horses of fire took Elijah up in Elisha's sight (2:11-12). Elisha called them "the chariots of Israel and its horsemen": God himself is Israel's true strength. Now they surround Elisha to protect him.

decisions.choice: the hill: the hill country around Dothan
decisions.reason: Dothan stood on a hill, with higher ground around it. The word can mean a single hill or the hill country; the fiery army filled the slopes around the prophet.

decisions.choice: the young man
decisions.reason: The word (na'ar) is the one used for "his servant" in verse 15; it means a young man, often one in service. Balanced and Readable keep "young man" here to show who is meant.

source.text: וַיֵּרְדוּ֮ אֵלָיו֒ וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֨ל אֱלִישָׁ֤ע אֶל־יְהוָה֙ וַיֹּאמַ֔ר הַךְ־נָ֥א אֶת־הַגּוֹי־הַזֶּ֖ה בַּסַּנְוֵרִ֑ים וַיַּכֵּ֥ם בַּסַּנְוֵרִ֖ים כִּדְבַ֥ר אֱלִישָֽׁע׃

records.literal_gloss: And they came down to him, and prayed Elisha to Yahweh and said, Strike, please, the nation the this with blindness. And he struck them with blindness according to [the] word of Elisha.

en.L: And they came down to him, and Elisha prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, "Strike this nation, please, with blindness." And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} struck them with blindness according to the word of Elisha.
en.B: As the Arameans came down toward him, Elisha prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Please strike these people with a blinding light." So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} struck them with a blinding light, as Elisha had asked.
en.R: When the Arameans came down toward him, Elisha prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. He said, "Please make these men unable to see." So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} made them unable to see, just as Elisha had asked.

decisions.choice: blindness: a sudden dazzling or confusion
decisions.reason: The word (sanwerim) occurs only here and in Genesis 19:11, where the men of Sodom are struck at Lot's door. Here the soldiers can still walk and follow Elisha, but they do not recognize him or where they are (verses 19-20). It seems to be a sudden blinding or bewildering rather than ordinary blindness.

decisions.choice: they came down to him: the Arameans came toward Elisha
decisions.reason: The Arameans are the ones who move down toward Elisha to seize him. Some take it as Elisha going down toward them, but the next words fit best with the enemy approaching.

decisions.choice: this nation: this army
decisions.reason: The word usually means a nation or people. Here it means the Aramean force that has come against him.

decisions.choice: a blinding light
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "a blinding light" to suggest a sudden dazzling rather than lasting blindness, as in Genesis 19:11; Literal keeps "blindness", and Readable says they could not see.

decisions.choice: the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable names the LORD where the Hebrew says only "he struck them".

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֜ם אֱלִישָׁ֗ע לֹ֣א זֶ֣ה הַדֶּרֶךְ֮ וְלֹ֣א זֹ֣ה הָעִיר֒ לְכ֣וּ אַחֲרַ֔י וְאוֹלִ֣יכָה אֶתְכֶ֔ם אֶל־הָאִ֖ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תְּבַקֵּשׁ֑וּן וַיֹּ֥לֶךְ אוֹתָ֖ם שֹׁמְרֽוֹנָה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to them Elisha, Not this [is] the way, and not this [is] the city; come after me, and I will lead you to the man whom you seek. And he led them to Samaria.

en.L: And Elisha said to them, "This [is] not the way, and this [is] not the city. Come after me, and I will lead you to the man whom you seek." And he led them to Samaria.
en.B: Elisha said to them, "This is not the right road, and this is not the town. Come after me, and I will lead you to the man you are seeking." So he brought them to Samaria.
en.R: Elisha said to them, "This is the wrong road, and this is the wrong town. Come with me. I will take you to the person you want." Then he led them all the way to Samaria.

decisions.choice: not the way, not the city: Elisha leads the blinded army away
decisions.reason: Elisha's words mislead the soldiers, yet in the end they are true: the man they seek is Elisha himself, and he does bring them to himself, in Samaria. He uses the trick to spare lives, not to destroy (verses 21-23).

decisions.choice: Samaria: Israel's capital
decisions.reason: Samaria, about 10 miles south of Dothan, was the walled capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:24). There the Arameans would be at the mercy of Israel's king.

decisions.choice: the wrong road; the wrong town
decisions.reason: Readable states the same thing in the most direct words.

source.text: וַיְהִי֮ כְּבֹאָ֣ם שֹׁמְרוֹן֒ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלִישָׁ֔ע יְהוָ֕ה פְּקַ֥ח אֶת־עֵינֵֽי־אֵ֖לֶּה וְיִרְא֑וּ וַיִּפְקַ֤ח יְהוָה֙ אֶת־עֵ֣ינֵיהֶ֔ם וַיִּרְא֕וּ וְהִנֵּ֖ה בְּת֥וֹךְ שֹׁמְרֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, as they came [into] Samaria, and said Elisha, Yahweh, open [the] eyes of these, and they will see. And opened Yahweh their eyes, and they saw, and look, in [the] midst of Samaria.

en.L: And it happened, as they came [into] Samaria, that Elisha said, "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, open the eyes of these [men], so that they may see." And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} opened their eyes, and they saw, and look, [they were] in the middle of Samaria.
en.B: As soon as they entered Samaria, Elisha said, "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, open the eyes of these men so that they can see." {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} opened their eyes, and they looked and found that they were in the middle of Samaria.
en.R: As soon as they had entered Samaria, Elisha prayed, "{{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, open these men's eyes so that they can see." {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} opened their eyes. They looked around and saw that they were right in the middle of Samaria.

decisions.choice: open the eyes of these: the same prayer as for the servant
decisions.reason: Elisha uses the words he prayed for his servant in verse 17. The servant's eyes were opened to see God's protection; the Arameans' eyes are opened to see that they are trapped.

decisions.choice: look, in the middle of Samaria: what they saw
decisions.reason: The word "look" (hinneh) shows the scene from the soldiers' side: they suddenly find themselves inside the enemy's capital.

decisions.choice: prayed
decisions.reason: Readable says "prayed" because Elisha's words are spoken to the LORD, as in verses 17-18.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶל־אֱלִישָׁ֔ע כִּרְאֹת֖וֹ אוֹתָ֑ם הַאַכֶּ֥ה אַכֶּ֖ה אָבִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] king of Israel to Elisha when he saw them, Shall I strike? Shall I strike, my father?

en.L: And [the] king of Israel said to Elisha when he saw them, "Shall I strike [them]? Shall I strike [them], my father?"
en.B: When the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, "My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?"
en.R: When the king of Israel saw the Arameans, he asked Elisha, "My father, should I kill them? Should I kill them?"

decisions.choice: shall I strike, shall I strike: an eager request
decisions.reason: The repeated question shows the king's eagerness to kill the helpless soldiers; he waits only for the prophet's permission.

decisions.choice: my father: a title of respect for the prophet
decisions.reason: The king calls Elisha "father", as Elisha called Elijah (2:12) and as a later king calls Elisha (13:14). It honors him as a man of God with authority.

decisions.choice: the king of Israel: not named here
decisions.reason: The king is not named in this chapter. The king of Israel in these chapters is Joram son of Ahab (3:1).

decisions.choice: kill
decisions.reason: "Strike" here means strike down, that is, kill; Balanced and Readable say so.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ לֹ֣א תַכֶּ֔ה הַאֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁבִ֛יתָ בְּחַרְבְּךָ֥ וּֽבְקַשְׁתְּךָ֖ אַתָּ֣ה מַכֶּ֑ה שִׂים֩ לֶ֨חֶם וָמַ֜יִם לִפְנֵיהֶ֗ם וְיֹֽאכְלוּ֙ וְיִשְׁתּ֔וּ וְיֵלְכ֖וּ אֶל־אֲדֹנֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, Not you will strike; those whom you have captured with your sword and with your bow, [are] you striking? Set bread and water before them, and they will eat and drink, and they will go to their master.

en.L: And he said, "You shall not strike [them]. Would you strike those whom you have captured with your sword and with your bow? Set bread and water before them, so that they may eat and drink, and go to their master."
en.B: "Do not kill them," he answered. "Would you kill men you had captured with your own sword and bow? Set food and water before them, so that they can eat and drink and then go back to their master."
en.R: Elisha answered, "Do not kill them. You would not even kill soldiers you had captured in battle with your own sword and bow! Give them food and water. Let them eat and drink, and then let them go back to their master."

decisions.choice: would you strike those you captured: you do not kill such captives
alternatives: Are you in the habit of killing those you capture? (a question about his practice)
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "No". Even prisoners taken in battle were not simply put to death; still less these men, whom the LORD, not the king, has delivered into his hands.

decisions.choice: bread: food in general
decisions.reason: The word often means food of any kind (Genesis 3:19). Verse 23 shows it became a great meal.

decisions.choice: their master: the king of Aram
decisions.reason: The soldiers' master is the king who sent them (verse 14). The word is plural in form, as often for a master or lord.

decisions.choice: You would not even kill soldiers you had captured in battle
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into a statement so its point is plain.

source.text: וַיִּכְרֶ֨ה לָהֶ֜ם כֵּרָ֣ה גְדוֹלָ֗ה וַיֹּֽאכְלוּ֙ וַיִּשְׁתּ֔וּ וַֽיְשַׁלְּחֵ֔ם וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ אֶל־אֲדֹֽנֵיהֶ֑ם וְלֹֽא־יָ֤סְפוּ עוֹד֙ גְּדוּדֵ֣י אֲרָ֔ם לָב֖וֹא בְּאֶ֥רֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And he prepared for them a feast great, and they ate and drank, and he sent them away, and they went to their master; and not again came [the] raiding bands of Aram into [the] land of Israel.

en.L: And he prepared for them a great feast, and they ate and drank, and he sent them away, and they went to their master. And [the] raiding bands of Aram did not come again into [the] land of Israel.
en.B: So the king prepared a great feast for them. When they had finished eating and drinking, he let them go, and they returned to their master. And the Aramean raiding bands did not come into the land of Israel again.
en.R: So the king prepared a big feast for them. When they had finished eating and drinking, he sent them home to their master. After that, the Aramean raiders stopped coming into Israel's land.

decisions.choice: he prepared a feast: a rare word for a banquet
decisions.reason: The verb and noun used here for preparing a feast are found only in this verse. They describe a large meal, far more than the bread and water Elisha asked for.

decisions.choice: raiding bands: small groups of raiders
decisions.reason: The word means troops sent out to raid (5:2, where such a band carried off the Israelite girl). Verse 24 tells of a full war later; what stopped was the raiding for now.

decisions.choice: he sent them away: mercy instead of killing
decisions.reason: Elisha's command turns enemies into guests. Their safe return, rather than slaughter, brings a time of peace from raids.

decisions.choice: the king
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the king as the one who prepared the feast, since the Hebrew says only "he".

source.text: וַֽיְהִי֙ אַחֲרֵי־כֵ֔ן וַיִּקְבֹּ֛ץ בֶּן־הֲדַ֥ד מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֖ם אֶת־כָּל־מַחֲנֵ֑הוּ וַיַּ֕עַל וַיָּ֖צַר עַל־שֹׁמְרֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was after thus, and gathered Ben-hadad, king of Aram, all his army, and went up and laid siege against Samaria.

en.L: And it happened after this that Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered all his army, and went up and laid siege against Samaria.
en.B: Some time after this, Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered his whole army, marched up, and laid siege to Samaria.
en.R: Some time later, Ben-hadad, the king of Aram, gathered his whole army. He marched against Samaria and surrounded the city to cut it off.

decisions.choice: Ben-hadad king of Aram: the ruler in Damascus
decisions.reason: Ben-hadad, "son of Hadad" (an Aramean god), was the name of more than one king of Damascus. This one had fought Ahab and besieged Samaria before (1 Kings 20:1).

decisions.choice: after this: a later time
decisions.reason: The words do not say how long after. The raiding bands had stopped (verse 23); now the king comes with his whole army, which is a different kind of war.

decisions.choice: laid siege: shut the city in
decisions.reason: In a siege an army surrounded a walled city and cut off its food and supplies until hunger forced it to give up (Deuteronomy 20:19; 28:52).

decisions.choice: surrounded the city to cut it off
decisions.reason: Readable explains what laying siege means.

source.text: וַיְהִ֨י רָעָ֤ב גָּדוֹל֙ בְּשֹׁ֣מְר֔וֹן וְהִנֵּ֖ה צָרִ֣ים עָלֶ֑יהָ עַ֣ד הֱי֤וֹת רֹאשׁ־חֲמוֹר֙ בִּשְׁמֹנִ֣ים כֶּ֔סֶף וְרֹ֛בַע הַקַּ֥ב דִּבְיוֹנִ֖יםבַּחֲמִשָּׁה־כָֽסֶף׃

records.literal_gloss: And there was a famine great in Samaria, and look, [they were] besieging it, until was [the] head of a donkey for eighty [of] silver, and [the] fourth of the kab of dove's dung for five [of] silver.

en.L: And there was a great famine in Samaria, and look, [they were] besieging it until a donkey's head was [sold] for eighty [shekels of] silver, and the fourth of a kab of dove's dung for five [shekels of] silver.
en.B: There was a great famine in Samaria. The siege went on so long that a donkey's head sold for {{units:about 2 pounds of silver|eighty shekels of silver}}, and {{units:about a cup|a quarter of a kab}} of dove's dung for {{units:about 2 ounces of silver|five shekels of silver}}.
en.R: There was a terrible famine in Samaria. The siege lasted so long that a donkey's head cost {{units:about 2 pounds of silver|eighty pieces of silver}}. A small bowl of dove's dung, {{units:about a cup|a quarter of a kab}}, cost {{units:about 2 ounces of silver|five pieces of silver}}.

decisions.choice: a donkey's head: the poorest of food
decisions.reason: The donkey was an unclean animal under the law (Leviticus 11:2-8), and the head has little meat. That it fetched such a price shows how desperate the people were.

decisions.choice: dove's dung: either droppings or a plant with that name
decisions.reason: The word means "doves' dung". It may be meant literally, as a sign of extreme hunger, perhaps for fuel or salt as well as food. But it may also be the popular name of a wild plant, such as the bulb of a small lily or a kind of pod or pea, eaten only in hard times. The evidence does not settle it.

decisions.choice: the written text and the reading aloud
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the Hebrew text give a coarser word for dung; the scribes' note in the margin directs a politer word to be read aloud. Both mean the same thing.

decisions.choice: silver and the kab: the prices and the measure
decisions.reason: "Eighty of silver" means eighty shekels; a shekel weighed about 2/5 ounce. A kab was a small dry measure, about a quart; a quarter of it is about a cup. Both prices are huge for such things.

decisions.choice: units spans for the shekels and the kab
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give modern weights and measures, with the original units as the alternative; Literal keeps the Hebrew units. Readable says "pieces of silver" in its alternative and adds "a small bowl" to picture the amount.

source.text: וַֽיְהִי֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל עֹבֵ֖ר עַל־הַחֹמָ֑ה וְאִשָּׁ֗ה צָעֲקָ֤ה אֵלָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הוֹשִׁ֖יעָה אֲדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And was [the] king of Israel passing on the wall, and a woman cried out to him, saying, Save, my lord the king.

en.L: And [the] king of Israel was passing by on the wall, and a woman cried out to him, saying, "Save [me], my lord the king!"
en.B: The king of Israel was passing by on the city wall when a woman called out to him, "Help, my lord the king!"
en.R: One day the king of Israel was walking along the top of the city wall. A woman shouted to him, "Please help me, Your Majesty!"

decisions.choice: passing on the wall: inspecting the defenses
decisions.reason: City walls were thick, with a walkway on top. During a siege the king would walk there to see the enemy and check on his guards.

decisions.choice: save: rescue, help
decisions.reason: The cry "Save!" was a plea to the king for help or justice (2 Samuel 14:4). The king hears it as a call to rescue her from hunger (verse 27), but she has a case to bring.

decisions.choice: Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Readable uses the modern way to address a king for "my lord the king".

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אַל־יוֹשִׁעֵ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה מֵאַ֖יִן אֽוֹשִׁיעֵ֑ךְ הֲמִן־הַגֹּ֖רֶן א֥וֹ מִן־הַיָּֽקֶב׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, Not let save you Yahweh, from where will I save you? From the threshing floor or from the winepress?

en.L: And he said, "[If] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} does not save you, from where will I save you? From the threshing floor, or from the winepress?"
en.B: He said, "If {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} does not help you, where could I get help for you? From the threshing floor, or from the winepress?"
en.R: The king answered, "If {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} does not help you, how can I help you? Do I have any grain or wine to give you?"

decisions.choice: if the LORD does not save you: a bitter answer
decisions.reason: The words can be read as a condition, "If Yahweh does not save you", or as a wish, "No! Let Yahweh save you". Either way the king says that only Yahweh can help, and he cannot.

decisions.choice: the threshing floor, the winepress: the sources of grain and wine
decisions.reason: The threshing floor gave grain and the winepress gave wine and oil (Numbers 18:27; Hosea 9:2). The king means that both are empty: he has no food to give.

decisions.choice: Do I have any grain or wine to give you?
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the threshing floor and winepress stand for.

source.text: וַיֹּֽאמֶר־לָ֥הּ הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מַה־לָּ֑ךְ וַתֹּ֗אמֶר הָאִשָּׁ֨ה הַזֹּ֜את אָמְרָ֣ה אֵלַ֗י תְּנִ֤י אֶת־בְּנֵךְ֙ וְנֹאכְלֶ֣נּוּ הַיּ֔וֹם וְאֶת־בְּנִ֖י נֹאכַ֥ל מָחָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to her the king, What to you? And she said, The woman the this said to me, Give your son and we will eat him today, and my son we will eat tomorrow.

en.L: And the king said to her, "What [is the matter] with you?" And she said, "This woman said to me, 'Give your son, so that we may eat him today, and my son we will eat tomorrow.'
en.B: Then the king asked her, "What is the matter?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give up your son, so that we can eat him today, and tomorrow we will eat my son.'
en.R: Then the king asked, "What is wrong?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give us your son to eat today, and tomorrow we will eat my son.'

decisions.choice: eating their children: the curse of the siege
decisions.reason: Moses warned that if Israel broke the covenant, an enemy siege would drive people to eat their own children (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57, where a gentle woman hides and eats her child). The horror shows how far the covenant's curses had come on Samaria (Lamentations 4:10).

decisions.choice: this woman: two women before a king
decisions.reason: The scene recalls the two women who came to Solomon about a child (1 Kings 3:16-27). There the king's wisdom saved the child; here the king can do nothing.

decisions.choice: the speech runs into verse 29
decisions.reason: The woman's words continue in the next record, so the quotation stays open at the end of this one.

source.text: וַנְּבַשֵּׁ֥ל אֶת־בְּנִ֖י וַנֹּֽאכְלֵ֑הוּ וָאֹמַ֨ר אֵלֶ֜יהָ בַּיּ֣וֹם הָאַחֵ֗ר תְּנִ֤י אֶת־בְּנֵךְ֙ וְנֹ֣אכְלֶ֔נּוּ וַתַּחְבִּ֖א אֶת־בְּנָֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And we cooked my son and we ate him; and I said to her on the day the other, Give your son and we will eat him; and she hid her son.

en.L: And we cooked my son and ate him. And I said to her on the next day, 'Give your son, so that we may eat him'; but she has hidden her son."
en.B: So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day I said to her, 'Give up your son, so that we can eat him.' But she has hidden her son."
en.R: So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day I said to her, 'Now give us your son to eat.' But she has hidden him."

decisions.choice: she hid her son: she has hidden him
decisions.reason: The woman complains that the other broke their agreement. The verb tells what the other woman did, and the son is still hidden as she speaks.

decisions.choice: the woman's complaint: the depth of the city's ruin
decisions.reason: She asks the king for justice in a bargain that should never have been made. The story shows how hunger has destroyed even a mother's love, as the covenant curse said (Deuteronomy 28:56-57).

decisions.choice: she has hidden him
decisions.reason: Readable uses "him" for "her son", since the son was just named.

source.text: וַיְהִי֩ כִשְׁמֹ֨עַ הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֤י הָֽאִשָּׁה֙ וַיִּקְרַ֣ע אֶת־בְּגָדָ֔יו וְה֖וּא עֹבֵ֣ר עַל־הַחֹמָ֑ה וַיַּ֣רְא הָעָ֔ם וְהִנֵּ֥ה הַשַּׂ֛ק עַל־בְּשָׂר֖וֹ מִבָּֽיִת׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, when heard the king the words of the woman, and he tore his clothes, and he [was] passing on the wall; and saw the people, and look, the sackcloth [was] on his flesh underneath.

en.L: And it happened, when the king heard the words of the woman, that he tore his clothes, as he was passing by on the wall; and the people looked, and look, the sackcloth [was] on his body underneath.
en.B: When the king heard what the woman said, he tore his clothes. As he passed by on the wall, the people saw that he was wearing sackcloth underneath, against his skin.
en.R: When the king heard what the woman said, he tore his royal clothes in grief. He was still walking on the wall, so the people could see that under his clothes he was wearing rough sackcloth.

decisions.choice: he tore his clothes: a sign of grief and horror
decisions.reason: Tearing one's clothes showed deep grief or shock (2 Samuel 13:31; 2 Kings 5:7).

decisions.choice: sackcloth underneath: mourning worn in secret
decisions.reason: Sackcloth was rough cloth of goat hair worn in mourning or to show sorrow before God (1 Kings 21:27). The king wore it under his royal robes, out of sight; the tear let the people see it.

decisions.choice: the king's sackcloth: grief without trust
decisions.reason: The sackcloth shows the king was mourning and perhaps seeking God's mercy, yet in the next verse he turns his anger on God's prophet. His outward sorrow and his inner bitterness stand side by side.

decisions.choice: in grief; rough
decisions.reason: Readable adds why he tore his clothes and what sackcloth was like.

source.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר כֹּֽה־יַעֲשֶׂה־לִּ֥י אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְכֹ֣ה יוֹסִ֑ף אִֽם־יַעֲמֹ֞ד רֹ֣אשׁ אֱלִישָׁ֧ע בֶּן־שָׁפָ֛ט עָלָ֖יו הַיּֽוֹם׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, Thus may do to me God and thus may he add, if will stand [the] head of Elisha son of Shaphat on him the day.

en.L: And he said, "Thus may God do to me, and thus may {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} add, if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat stays on him today."
en.B: He said, "May God deal with me ever so severely if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat stays on his shoulders today!"
en.R: He said, "May God punish me terribly if Elisha son of Shaphat still has his head on his shoulders by the end of today!"

decisions.choice: thus may God do to me, and thus may he add: a solemn oath
decisions.reason: This is the form of a curse the speaker calls down on himself if he does not do what he says (1 Samuel 3:17; 20:13; Ruth 1:17). The punishment is left unnamed. The king swears to have Elisha beheaded that day.

decisions.choice: why the king blames Elisha
decisions.reason: The text does not say why. The king seems to hold God's prophet responsible for the disaster, perhaps because Elisha had urged him to hold out and wait for God's help (verse 33), or because he thought the prophet could end the siege and would not. Like his father Ahab, he blames the prophet for the trouble (1 Kings 18:17).

decisions.choice: ever so severely; punish me terribly
decisions.reason: The oath uses the same wording at each level as in 1 Samuel 3:17 and 20:13: Literal keeps the Hebrew form, Balanced "deal with me ever so severely", Readable "punish me terribly".

source.text: וֶאֱלִישָׁע֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב בְּבֵית֔וֹ וְהַזְּקֵנִ֖ים יֹשְׁבִ֣ים אִתּ֑וֹ וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח אִ֜ישׁ מִלְּפָנָ֗יו בְּטֶ֣רֶם יָבֹא֩ הַמַּלְאָ֨ךְ אֵלָ֜יו וְה֣וּא׀אָמַ֣ר אֶל־הַזְּקֵנִ֗ים הַרְּאִיתֶם֙ כִּֽי־שָׁלַ֞ח בֶּן־הַֽמְרַצֵּ֤חַ הַזֶּה֙ לְהָסִ֣יר אֶת־רֹאשִׁ֔י רְא֣וּ׀כְּבֹ֣א הַמַּלְאָ֗ךְ סִגְר֤וּ הַדֶּ֨לֶת֙ וּלְחַצְתֶּ֤ם אֹתוֹ֙ בַּדֶּ֔לֶת הֲל֗וֹא ק֛וֹל רַגְלֵ֥י אֲדֹנָ֖יו אַחֲרָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And Elisha [was] sitting in his house, and the elders [were] sitting with him; and he sent a man from before him; before came the messenger to him, and he said to the elders, Do you see that has sent [the] son of the murderer the this to remove my head? Look, when comes the messenger, shut the door, and press him with the door; [is] not [the] sound of [the] feet of his master behind him?

en.L: And Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. And [the king] sent a man from before him; before the messenger came to him, he said to the elders, "Do you see that this son of a murderer has sent to remove my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and press him back with the door. [Is] not the sound of his master's feet behind him?"
en.B: Now Elisha was at home, with the elders sitting beside him. The king sent a man ahead of him, but before the messenger arrived, Elisha told the elders, "Do you see? This son of a murderer has sent someone to take off my head. Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and hold it shut against him. Is not the sound of his master's footsteps right behind him?"
en.R: Meanwhile Elisha was sitting in his house, and the leaders of the city were sitting with him. The king sent a man ahead to kill Elisha. But before the man arrived, Elisha said to the leaders, "Do you see? This son of a murderer has sent someone to cut off my head! When the messenger comes, shut the door and keep him out. His master, the king, is coming right behind him."

decisions.choice: this son of a murderer: the son of Ahab
decisions.reason: The king was a son of Ahab (3:1), who had Naboth put to death to take his vineyard (1 Kings 21:1-19). Elisha means that the son is like the father: a man who kills an innocent man.

decisions.choice: Do you see: Elisha knows before the man arrives
decisions.reason: As he knew the Aramean king's plans (verse 12), Elisha knows the king's order before the messenger reaches the house.

decisions.choice: the elders: the leaders of the city
decisions.reason: The elders were the senior men who led the city's affairs (1 Kings 21:8). That they sit with Elisha shows how much they look to him in the crisis.

decisions.choice: the sound of his master's feet behind him: the king is coming too
decisions.reason: Elisha's question expects the answer "Yes": the king himself is following his messenger. This prepares for verse 33 and 7:2, where the king and his officer are present.

decisions.choice: the king
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "he sent". Balanced and Readable name the king, as verse 31 shows.

decisions.choice: to kill Elisha; the leaders of the city
decisions.reason: Readable states the messenger's purpose, which Elisha's words make clear, and calls the elders "leaders of the city".

source.text: עוֹדֶ֨נּוּ֙ מְדַבֵּ֣ר עִמָּ֔ם וְהִנֵּ֥ה הַמַּלְאָ֖ךְ יֹרֵ֣ד אֵלָ֑יו וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הִנֵּֽה־זֹ֤את הָֽרָעָה֙ מֵאֵ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה מָֽה־אוֹחִ֥יל לַיהוָ֖ה עֽוֹד׃ס

records.literal_gloss: While he [was] speaking with them, and look, the messenger [was] coming down to him; and he said, Look, this the trouble [is] from Yahweh; why will I wait for Yahweh still?

en.L: While he was still speaking with them, look, the messenger was coming down to him. And he said, "Look, this trouble [is] from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Why should I wait for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} any longer?"
en.B: Elisha was still talking with them when the messenger came down to him. And he said, "This disaster comes from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Why should I go on waiting for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"
en.R: While Elisha was still talking with them, the messenger arrived. He said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has brought this trouble on us. Why should I keep waiting for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to help?"

decisions.choice: the messenger came down, and he said: the words are the king's
alternatives: the king came down to him
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says the messenger arrived and "he said". The words sound like the king's own (7:2 shows the king and his officer there), and Elisha has just said the king is following close behind (verse 32). The messenger may be bringing the king's words, or the king himself may speak as he arrives. Some suggest the word "messenger" was first "king", since the two words look alike in Hebrew.

decisions.choice: this trouble is from Yahweh: despair, not trust
decisions.reason: The speaker rightly sees that the disaster comes from Yahweh, but draws the opposite lesson from faith: since Yahweh has done this, there is no point in hoping in him any longer.

decisions.choice: wait for Yahweh: hope for his help
decisions.reason: To wait for Yahweh means to keep hoping and trusting that he will act (Psalm 130:5; Isaiah 40:31). The king's sackcloth (verse 30) may have been part of such waiting, which he now gives up.

decisions.choice: to help
decisions.reason: Readable adds what the speaker was waiting for.
